meaning: Marks the topic or subject an action is about, like “about” or “regarding”. More formal than 「〜について」.
connection: Noun + に関して(は)／に関する + noun

senses.label: About ... (adverbial)
senses.meaning: Shows what you talk, think, or investigate about. Like “about”, “regarding”, or “concerning”. The tone is formal, common in writing and business. 「〜に関しては」 sets up a topic, often with a contrastive feel.
senses.connection: Noun + に関して／に関しては + verb (説明する, 調べる, 質問する, etc.)
examples: Do you have any questions about this matter?
I wrote a report on environmental problems.
As for the fees, I'll explain them later.

senses.label: Noun + related to ...
senses.meaning: Modifies a noun: “... about X” or “... related to X”. Common with nouns like 「調査」, 「情報」, 「資料」, and 「法律」. 「〜に関しての」 also works.
senses.connection: Noun + に関する／に関しての + noun
examples: I'm reading a book about Japanese history.
The law on personal information was revised.

senses.label: Polite and written forms
senses.meaning: 「〜に関しまして」 is a more polite version, used in speeches and customer service. 「〜に関し、」 is a written linking form, common in official documents and the news.
senses.connection: Noun + に関しまして／に関し、
examples: Let me tell you about our new product.
The government began a detailed investigation into the accident.

notes: To modify a noun, use 「〜に関する」 or 「〜に関しての」. The te-form cannot attach directly to a noun: ✕「環境に関して問題」→ ○「環境に関する問題」.

It only means “about” a topic or content. It does not mark the person or thing an attitude or action is aimed at: 「先生に対して失礼だ」 is “rude toward the teacher”, but 「先生に関して」 turns it into “about the teacher”, and the meaning changes.
The tone is formal, like giving a report. Saying 「週末に関して話そう」 to a friend sounds stiff. Use ○「週末のこと、話そう」 or 「週末について話そう」.

「〜に関しては」 carries a contrastive “as far as this matter goes (leaving others aside)” feel. If you reply to a client with only 「この件に関しては…」, it may sound like you are holding something back. Formal replies often use 「〜に関しましては」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports often introduce a topic with 「〜に関して」.
daily.example: Apparently the government will make an announcement about this issue tomorrow.

daily.title: Looking for books at the library
daily.description: Asking a librarian for books on a certain topic.
daily.example: Where are the books about Japanese cooking?

work.title: Asking a question in a meeting
work.description: Asking the person in charge about an item on the agenda.
work.example: Let me just confirm one thing about the schedule.

work.title: Writing a business email
work.description: Telling the other party how a matter stands.
work.example: We will contact you again regarding the delivery date.

work.title: Customer service
work.description: Staff explaining what kinds of inquiries they handle.
work.example: For inquiries about your order, please contact us here.

etymology: 「関する」 is the Sino-Japanese word 「関」 plus the verb 「する」. 「関」 originally meant “barrier” or “checkpoint”, and came to mean “to be connected with”. 「〜に関して」 is its te-form, and 「〜に関する」 is the form that modifies nouns.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning, and usually interchangeable. 「〜について」 works in both speech and writing. 「〜に関して」 is more formal, common in reports, news, and business emails. To modify a noun, both 「〜についての」 and 「〜に関する」 work; the latter is more written.

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: Also means “around ...”, but is usually followed by words for disputes between several parties, such as 「議論する」, 「争う」, and 「対立する」: 「遺産をめぐって争う」. 「〜に関して」 just neutrally introduces a topic and can be followed by anything, such as an explanation or a question.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: Often compared. 「〜に対して」 marks the target of an attitude, action, or feeling (“toward ...”): 「客に対して丁寧だ」. 「〜に関して」 marks the topic (“about ...”). 「客に関して」 only means “about the customer” and cannot express an attitude toward the customer.

formation: Made of 「に」 (the target) + 「関し」 (the continuative form of the suru-verb 「関する」) + 「て」. 「関する」 comes from the Sino-Japanese word 「関」 (connection, involvement), so 「Aに関する」 means “to involve A, to be connected with A”. With the te-form 「関して」 linking to the next clause, it shows that explaining, investigating, asking, and so on are done “around matters connected with A”, which gives “about A”. The attributive form 「関する」 modifies a noun directly: “... connected with A”. Because its core is the Sino-Japanese 「関」, the whole expression is more written and formal than 「〜について」, which is built from a native Japanese verb.

meaning: Compares something against a standard, like “compared to ...” or “compared with ...”.
connection: Noun + に比べて／に比べ／と比べて

senses.label: Compared to ...
senses.meaning: Sets the first item as the standard and describes how the second item differs in degree. Like “compared to ...”. The second half usually has an adjective or a word of change. In writing, 「〜に比べ、」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun (verb phrase + の) + に比べて／に比べ、／と比べて
examples: This summer is hotter than last year.
Compared to Tokyo, prices in Osaka are low.
Compared to his older brother, the younger brother is quiet.

senses.label: If you compare it ...
senses.meaning: 「〜に比べると／比べれば／比べたら」 has a conditional feel: “if you compare it with ...”. Often used to say “... is nothing compared to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に比べると／に比べれば／に比べたら
examples: Compared to the past, the number of children has dropped a lot.
Compared to his hardships, mine are nothing.

notes: The two things compared must be parallel: ✕「日本の物価に比べて、中国は安い」 (comparing “prices” with “China”) → ○「日本に比べて、中国は物価が安い」 or 「日本の物価に比べて、中国の物価は安い」.
Don't mix it up with the verb's basic use. The basic use is 「AとBを比べる」 (to compare A and B). This pattern is 「Bに比べて、Aは〜」 (with B as the baseline): ✕「去年を比べて、今年は暑い」.
The second clause must state a difference in degree (an adjective, a change, etc.). It cannot be a plain action unrelated to the comparison: ✕「兄に比べて、弟は東京に住んでいる」→ ○「兄と違って、弟は東京に住んでいる」.
「〜に比べれば」 often implies “compared with ..., it's nothing”. Using it to compare the other person's hardship with your own (「あなたの苦労なんて、私に比べれば…」) belittles them and is very rude.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Comparing this year's weather with usual years while chatting with a neighbor.
daily.example: There's less snow this year than usual, isn't there?

daily.title: After moving
daily.description: Telling a friend how your new place differs from the old one.
daily.example: Compared to my old apartment, this one is close to the station and convenient.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Common when the news presents statistics.
daily.example: The number of travelers rose 20% compared to the previous year.

work.title: Reporting sales figures
work.description: Reporting this month's results compared with last month to your boss.
work.example: Sales this month grew 10% compared to last month.

work.title: Writing an analysis report
work.description: Comparing a new plan with the old one in a report.
work.example: The new method costs less than the conventional one.

etymology: 「比べる」 originally means “to put two things side by side and check them”. 「〜に比べて」 is its te-form, used to set the first item as the standard. The old form 「くらぶ」 also meant “to compete”.

similar.title: 〜は〜より〜 (comparison)
similar.explanation: 「AはBより〜」 is the most basic comparative sentence and is common in speech. 「Bに比べて、Aは〜」 puts more weight on “taking B as the baseline”, sounds a bit more formal, and is common when describing changes or statistics.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: 「BよりAのほうが〜」 is used for choosing between two, clearly stating which one is more ... . 「〜に比べて」 describes the gap more objectively and is not necessarily an either-or answer.

similar.title: 〜とは比べものにならない
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built on 「比べる」). 「〜とは比べものにならない」 says the gap is so big there is no comparison at all, and the tone is strong. 「〜に比べて」 is just an ordinary comparison.

similar.title: 〜にひきかえ
similar.explanation: Also means “compared with ...”, but only for contrasting two opposite situations, and it carries the speaker's praise, criticism, or feelings: 「兄にひきかえ、弟は怠け者だ」. 「〜に比べて」 just neutrally compares degree.

formation: Made of 「に」 (the baseline of comparison) + 「比べ」 (the verb 「比べる」: to set two things side by side) + 「て」. 「比べる」 originally lists two items equally, as in 「AとBを比べる」. 「Bに比べて」 puts B in the position of the baseline, and the next clause talks only about A, giving the structure “taking B as a reference, A is ...”. The te-form sets up the comparison as a premise, and the next clause gives the result directly, so it must be a difference in degree or state. The conditional forms 「比べると／比べれば」 add a nuance of “once you compare”, which easily leads to the meaning “compared with ..., it's nothing”.

meaning: Shows that a result goes against expectations or hopes, or that something breaks a rule or someone's will. Like “contrary to ...” or “against ...”.
connection: Noun + に反して／に反し／に反する + noun

senses.label: Contrary to expectations
senses.meaning: The actual result is the opposite of what was expected or hoped for. Like “contrary to ...”. Often used with 「予想」, 「期待」, and 「予測」.
senses.connection: 予想／期待／予測／見通し + に反して／に反し、／に反した + noun
examples: Contrary to expectations, the Japanese team won the match.
Against his parents' hopes, he quit university.
The result went against most people's predictions.

senses.label: Against (a rule)
senses.meaning: Shows that something breaks a rule, law, moral, or someone's will. Like “against ...” or “in violation of ...”. Use 「〜に反する」 before a noun.
senses.connection: 規則／法律／ルール／意思 + に反する + noun／に反して
examples: That is an act against the law.
The operation was performed against the patient's will.

notes: Don't confuse it with 「〜に反対する」: 「計画に反対する」 is “to oppose the plan” (stating a position), while 「計画に反して」 is “contrary to the plan, violating the plan”. The meanings are completely different.
It follows nouns for expectations, hopes, rules, or wishes (「予想」, 「期待」, 「規則」, 「意思」). It cannot contrast two people or things: ✕「兄に反して、弟は背が高い」→ ○「兄と違って、弟は背が高い」.
When it means “contrary to expectations”, the second clause is a result that has already happened. It cannot be a request or an intention: ✕「予想に反して、頑張ってください」.
When apologizing to a superior or client, the usual phrase is 「ご期待に沿えず、申し訳ございません」. 「ご期待に反して」 only states that “the result went against your expectations” and is not appropriate as an apology.

daily.title: Talking about a test
daily.description: Telling a friend about a surprising test result.
daily.example: Contrary to what I expected, the test was easy.

daily.title: Reading sports news
daily.description: Sports news reporting an upset.
daily.example: Against most predictions, a rookie won the championship.

work.title: Analyzing results
work.description: Explaining in a meeting that results fell short of expectations.
work.example: Contrary to our hopes, the new product did not sell well.

work.title: Internal company notice
work.description: Reminding employees to follow company rules.
work.example: Any conduct that violates company rules will be dealt with strictly.

etymology: 「反する」 is the Sino-Japanese word 「反」 plus 「する」. 「反」 originally means “to turn over” or “opposite”. 「〜に反して」 is literally “going the opposite way to ...”, which led to “contrary to expectations” and “against the rules”.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Both can show an unexpected result. 「〜にもかかわらず」 follows an established fact (“even though it rained”) and shows that the fact had no effect. 「〜に反して」 follows the expectation itself and shows that the result went the other way: 「予想に反して」.

similar.title: 〜のに (contrast)
similar.explanation: Both can show something contrary to expectations. 「のに」 attaches to a full clause, is spoken and subjective, and often carries dissatisfaction or regret. 「〜に反して」 only follows nouns like 「予想」 and 「期待」, and sounds written and objective.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「〜のに対して」 can objectively contrast two different things (「兄が活発なのに対して、弟はおとなしい」). 「〜に反して」 stresses that a result “goes against” an expectation or a rule, and is not used to set two things side by side.

formation: Made of 「に」 (what something is set against) + 「反し」 (the continuative form of the suru-verb 「反する」) + 「て」. 「反」 is a Sino-Japanese element whose basic meaning is “to turn over, reverse”, so 「Aに反する」 means “to go the opposite way from A”. When A is an expectation or hope, a result going the opposite way means “unexpectedly, contrary to expectations”. When A is a rule, law, or wish, an action going the opposite way means “to violate, go against”. Both senses come from the same structure; the only difference is whether A is an expectation or a norm. The attributive forms 「反する」 and 「反した」 modify nouns directly: 「法律に反する行為」.

meaning: Shows that someone does something in place of another person, or that something new replaces something old. Like “on behalf of ...” or “in place of ...”.
connection: Noun + に代わって／に代わり／に代わる + noun

senses.label: On behalf of someone
senses.meaning: Someone else does what a certain person would normally do. Like “on behalf of ...” or “in place of ...”. The tone is formal, often used in speeches and statements.
senses.connection: Person + に代わって／に代わり(まして)
examples: I will give the greeting on behalf of our president.
My older sister is doing the housework in place of our sick mother.

senses.label: Replacing something
senses.meaning: Something new has taken the place of something older. Like “replacing ...” or “instead of ...”. Use 「〜に代わる」 before a noun.
senses.connection: Noun + に代わって／に代わり、／に代わる + noun
examples: Email came to be used instead of letters.
We need new energy sources to replace oil.

notes: It sounds the same as 「〜に変わる」 (to change into ...), and writing the wrong kanji changes the meaning completely: 「社長に代わって挨拶する」 = to give a speech on behalf of the president; 「信号が青に変わる」 = the light turns green.
When speaking to outsiders on behalf of your boss, don't use honorifics for people in your own company: ✕「社長様に代わりまして」→ ○「社長の山田に代わりまして、ご挨拶申し上げます」.

For everyday, one-off personal substitutions (using tofu instead of meat), use 「〜の代わりに」: ✕「肉に代わって豆腐を使った」→ ○「肉の代わりに豆腐を使った」. When 「〜に代わって」 means “replacing”, it is mostly used for changes at the level of eras or society.

daily.title: Attending for a family member
daily.description: Explaining that you came in place of a family member.
daily.example: I came in place of my father.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reporting new technology replacing old technology.
daily.example: Smartphone payments are spreading and replacing cash.

work.title: Speaking for your boss in a meeting
work.description: Explaining things when your manager is absent.
work.example: Today I will explain on behalf of our department manager.

work.title: Writing a proposal
work.description: Proposing a new system to replace the old one.
work.example: We propose a new framework to replace the current system.

etymology: 「代わる」 means “to take the place of” or “to replace”. It shares a root with 「変わる」 (to change) and 「替わる」 (to switch). 「〜に代わって」 means stepping into someone's or something's place.

similar.title: 〜代わりに
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「代わる」). 「〜の代わりに」 has a wider range: it can also mean “do B instead of A”, “in exchange”, or “there are pros and cons”. 「〜に代わって」 only means substituting or replacing, sounds more solemn, and is mostly used in speeches and formal writing.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: When attending for someone, people also often say 「社長の代理として出席する」 (to attend as the president's representative). 「〜として」 means doing something in a certain role, focusing on the role. 「社長に代わって」 focuses on doing for the president what he would normally do himself.

formation: Made of 「に」 (the person or thing being replaced, i.e. the position) + 「代わっ」 (the verb 「代わる」: to replace, take over) + 「て」. 「Aに代わる」 literally means “to switch into A's place”: to stand where A stood and take on A's role. When the subject is a person, it means doing what A should have done (“on behalf of A”). When the subject is a thing, it means something new taking the place of the old A (“replacing A”). The te-form links to the next clause: “doing ... in place of A”. The attributive 「〜に代わる + noun」 means “... that can replace A”, and the suspended form 「〜に代わり」 is more written.

meaning: Shows substitution, doing one thing instead of another, an exchange, or a trade-off between good and bad points. Like “instead of ...” or “in exchange for ...”.
connection: Noun + の／verb plain form／adjective + 代わりに

senses.label: Instead of (substitute)
senses.meaning: Uses another person or thing as a substitute. Like “instead of ...”. 「代わりに」 alone can also be an adverb meaning “instead” or “for me”.
senses.connection: Noun + の代わりに
examples: I used tofu instead of meat.
I attended the meeting in place of my father.

senses.label: Do B instead of A
senses.meaning: Instead of doing the first thing, you do the second. The first is usually what you would normally or should do. Like “instead of doing ..., ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／ない-form + 代わりに
examples: Instead of complaining, I fixed it myself.
Instead of eating out today, let's cook at home.

senses.label: In exchange
senses.meaning: You do the second thing in exchange for, or to make up for, the first. Like “in return”. At the start of a sentence, use 「その代わり(に)」.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + 代わりに／その代わり(に)
examples: In exchange for English lessons, I taught them Japanese.
I'll help you. In return, treat me to dinner, OK?

senses.label: Trade-off
senses.meaning: The first part has an advantage, but the second part has a matching downside (or the other way around). Like “..., but on the other hand ...”.
senses.connection: Adjective／verb plain form + 代わりに
examples: This shop is cheap, but the service isn't good.
The city is convenient, but the rent is high.

notes: A noun needs 「の」: ✕「母代わりに」→ ○「母の代わりに」. (As a noun, 「母代わり」 means “someone who looks after you like a mother”, which is a different meaning.)
In 「Aの代わりにB」, A is what gets replaced and B is what is actually used. Reverse them and the meaning is reversed: 「コーヒーの代わりに紅茶を飲んだ」 = I drank tea, not coffee.
In the “pros and cons” use, one side must be good and the other bad: ✕「この店は安い代わりに、おいしい」→ ○「この店は安い上に、おいしい」.
Using 「その代わり〜てください」 to set a condition for a superior or client sounds like haggling and is impolite. Say 「恐れ入りますが、〜ていただけますか」 instead.

daily.title: Swapping ingredients while cooking
daily.description: You're out of something, so you use something else.
daily.example: You can use soy milk instead of milk.

daily.title: Helping a friend
daily.description: Proposing a deal.
daily.example: I'll help with your homework if you buy me a juice.

daily.title: Comparing apartments
daily.description: Discussing the pros and cons of a place with family.
daily.example: This room is spacious, but it's far from the station.

work.title: Adjusting work days
work.description: Arranging a shift swap with a coworker.
work.example: I'll work on Saturday, so I'd like to take Monday off.

work.title: Going on a business trip for someone
work.description: A coworker can't go, so you go instead.
work.example: I'll go on the business trip to Osaka in place of Tanaka-san.

etymology: 「代わり」 is the noun made from the masu-stem of the verb 「代わる」, meaning “substitute” or “stand-in”. With 「に」 it became an adverbial phrase, “as a substitute”, which then grew into “in exchange” and “to make up for”.

similar.title: 〜に代わって・〜に代わり
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「代わる」). 「〜に代わって」 only means substituting or replacing, sounds solemn, and is mostly used in speeches (「社長に代わって」) and for changes of era. 「〜代わりに」 can also mean “do ... instead of ...”, “in exchange”, or “you gain something and lose something”. It has a wider range and is more conversational.

similar.title: 〜反面
similar.explanation: Close to the “pros and cons” use. 「〜反面」 objectively points out two opposite sides of the same thing and is somewhat written. 「〜代わりに」 stresses “the price for this benefit is ...”, with a sense of fair exchange.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: Can also contrast two sides of the same thing, but simply lists them, and they need not be one good and one bad. 「〜代わりに」 must be a trade-off of one gain for one loss.

formation: 「代わり」 is a noun made from the continuative form of the verb 「代わる」 (to replace), meaning “a substitute, a stand-in”. Adding 「に」 makes it adverbial: “as a substitute”. 「Aの代わりにB」 means “let B take A's place”. When A is a person or thing, it means “use B instead of A”. When A is an action you were going to do (「文句を言う代わりに」), it means “do B instead of doing A”. Read “substitution” as “fair compensation” and you get “do B in exchange for A”. Then treat an advantage and a disadvantage as canceling each other out, and you get “A has this benefit, but in return B has that drawback”. All four senses grow out of the core idea of replacement and compensation.

meaning: Shows a very confident, subjective judgment by the speaker. Like “must be ...” or “definitely ...”. Strong and rather conversational.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem／verb, i-adjective plain form + に決まっている

senses.label: It must be ...
senses.meaning: The speaker is sure, from common sense or experience, that things must be this way. Like “definitely” or “bound to”. It is a subjective judgment and needs no objective evidence.
senses.connection: Plain form + に決まっている／に決まってる (casual)
examples: We practiced this much, so we're sure to win.
A place that expensive is bound to be delicious.
A story like that is definitely a lie.

senses.label: Of course! (retort)
senses.meaning: Used to answer an obvious question, with a feel of “Do you even need to ask?”. Often 「〜に決まってるでしょ／じゃん」.
senses.connection: Plain form + に決まってるでしょ／に決まってるじゃん
examples: “Are you going?” “Of course I'm going!”
That's obviously impossible.

notes: The tone is subjective and dogmatic. Saying 「〜に決まっています」 to a superior or client sounds arrogant, as if you are dismissing them. In formal situations, use 「きっと〜と思います」 or 「〜に違いありません」.
「行くに決まってるでしょ」 carries an “isn't it obvious?” tone and is only for people you are close to. Answering an older person or a superior this way is very rude.
Nouns and na-adjectives attach directly, without 「だ」: ✕「うそだに決まっている」→ ○「うそに決まっている」; ✕「無理だに決まっている」→ ○「無理に決まっている」.

「会議は来週に決まった」 means “the meeting has been set for next week” (an objective decision, in the past tense). This pattern means “it's bound to be ...” (a subjective judgment, with 「ている」). Don't mix them up.

daily.title: A friend hesitating to confess their feelings
daily.description: Reassuring a friend with a strong guarantee.
daily.example: Don't worry, it's sure to go well.

daily.title: Family asking the obvious
daily.description: Mom asks if you want cake. Of course you do.
daily.example: “Want some cake?” “Of course I do!”

daily.title: Seeing through a suspicious offer
daily.description: Telling your family about a suspicious ad.
daily.example: A deal this good has to be a scam.

work.title: Chatting privately with a coworker
work.description: Judging a project's prospects with a close coworker.
work.example: With this deadline, there's no way we'll make it.

etymology: 「決まる」 means “to be settled” or “to be decided”. 「〜に決まっている」 literally means “it has been settled as ...”. The conclusion is fixed and beyond doubt, which became a strong assertion by the speaker.

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: Both express a confident guess. 「〜に違いない」 literally means “there can be no mistake”, is usually based on some evidence, and leans written. 「〜に決まっている」 leans spoken, is more subjective, and has a “naturally, of course” tone.

similar.title: 〜に相違ない
similar.explanation: Same meaning as 「〜に違いない」, but even more written and stiff, mostly seen in texts. 「〜に決まっている」 is a strong assertion in everyday speech, so the two are very far apart in register.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 「〜はずだ」 reasons from objective logic or facts to “it should be ...”, and is fairly calm. 「〜に決まっている」 is the speaker's own conviction, sounds stronger, and may have no basis at all.

similar.title: 〜と決まって
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built on 「決まる」), but different meaning: 「〜と決まって」 shows a pattern, “whenever ..., always ...” (「雨が降ると決まって頭が痛くなる」). It is not a judgment about a single case.

formation: Made of 「に」 (the end point or result) + 「決まっ」 (the verb 「決まる」: to be decided) + 「ている」 (a continuing resulting state). 「Aに決まる」 basically means “to be decided as A”, and adding 「ている」 gives “it has already been decided as A”. When the speaker uses it for something not actually confirmed, it amounts to declaring “the conclusion was settled as A long ago; there is no other possibility”, so it expresses a strong subjective judgment. Because it means “I have decided it is so”, it needs no objective evidence, so it naturally carries a “of course, needless to say” tone and sounds dogmatic.

meaning: Shows that over time you have adapted to or gotten used to something. Like “to get used to ...”.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + の(こと) + に慣れる

senses.label: Gradually getting used to
senses.meaning: Over time, you adapt to a new environment or something new. Like “get used to ...”. Often used with 「だんだん」, 「やっと」, and 「〜てきた」.
senses.connection: Noun + に慣れる／に慣れた／に慣れてきた
examples: I'm gradually getting used to life in Japan.
I've finally gotten used to my new job.

senses.label: Already used to (state)
senses.meaning: 「〜に慣れている」 means you are already used to or familiar with something. The negative 「〜に慣れていない」 means you aren't used to it yet.
senses.connection: Noun + に慣れている／に慣れていない
examples: He's used to speaking in front of people.
I'm not used to this computer yet.

senses.label: Used to doing something
senses.meaning: To use a verb, first turn it into a noun with 「〜のに慣れる」 or 「〜ことに慣れる」. It means you've gotten used to doing that action.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + の／こと + に慣れる
examples: I've gotten used to getting up early.
It took a while to get used to living alone.

notes: The particle is 「に」, not 「を」: ✕「日本の生活を慣れた」→ ○「日本の生活に慣れた」.
A verb must first be turned into a noun: ✕「早く起きるに慣れた」→ ○「早く起きるのに慣れた」 or 「早く起きることに慣れた」.
「〜に慣れる」 only means “to no longer find something hard or awkward”. It does not mean having a routine. For “I make a habit of running every morning”, say ○「毎朝走ることにしている」 or 「毎朝走る習慣がある」, not 「慣れる」.
Written in kana as 「〜になれる」, it can also be the potential form of 「なる」 (「医者になれる」 = can become a doctor). Be careful when a job or role comes before it, because the meaning is completely different.

daily.title: A student abroad
daily.description: Updating your family about life in Japan.
daily.example: I'm already used to the food here.

daily.title: Moving to a new city
daily.description: A friend asks how your new life is going.
daily.example: I'm still not used to packed trains, so I'm tired every day.

daily.title: Having a pet
daily.description: Talking about your newly adopted cat.
daily.example: It took a week for the cat to get used to the new house.

work.title: Check-in with a new employee
work.description: A manager asks how a new hire is settling in.
work.example: Have you gotten used to the work yet?

work.title: Describing your skills
work.description: Explaining your experience in a job interview.
work.example: I'm very used to dealing with overseas clients.

etymology: 「慣れる」 is also written 「馴れる」. Its original meaning is “to become familiar or close”, and 「馴」 is often used for tamed animals. From “becoming familiar through frequent contact”, it came to mean “to get used to” or “to adapt”.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: Both show a change over time and are often compared. 「〜ようになる」 shows an ability or habit appearing where there was none (“come to be able to ..., start to ...”). 「〜に慣れる」 shows mental or physical adjustment: you no longer find something hard or awkward.

similar.title: 〜ことにしている
similar.explanation: Both can sound like talking about a “habit”. 「〜ことにしている」 is a habit you decided on and stick to (“I make a point of ... every day”). 「〜に慣れる」 means you have adjusted to something; it does not mean a habit you actively built.

formation: Made of 「に」 (what you adjust to) + 「慣れる」 (an ichidan verb: to become familiar through repeated contact). 「慣れる」 describes a change in the subject itself: after repeated contact with something, you no longer find it strange, hard, or awkward. 「に」 shows which target this change happens toward, so the target takes 「に」, not 「を」. 「慣れる」 is a verb of change: 「慣れた」 = has become used to it, 「慣れている」 = is in a state of being used to it, 「慣れてきた」 = the change has gradually progressed up to now. Because 「に」 needs a noun before it, a verb must first be nominalized with 「の」 or 「こと」.

meaning: Says that the first item goes without saying and the second holds as well: “A goes without saying, and even B...”; 「はもちろん」 is the general form, while 「はもとより」 is more formal and written.
connection: Noun + はもちろん (のこと) / はもとより, noun + も / まで / さえ

senses.label: A, of course, and also B
senses.meaning: Gives an obvious example first, then says other things are the same. Like “not only A, of course, but also B”. The second half often has 「も」, 「まで」, or 「さえ」.
senses.connection: Noun + はもちろん、noun + も／まで
examples: This restaurant has great food, of course, and the service is good too.
He speaks English, of course, and Chinese as well.
It's crowded on weekends, of course, and even on weekdays.

senses.label: Emphatic: it goes without saying
senses.meaning: 「〜はもちろんのこと」 is stronger and more formal, common in writing and formal speeches.
senses.connection: Noun + はもちろんのこと、〜も
examples: It's a movie that adults can enjoy, not to mention children.
It is popular overseas, not to mention in Japan.

senses.label: はもとより (formal)
senses.meaning: A goes without saying, and so does B. Formal in tone; common in writing, speeches and notices. The second part often has 「も」 or 「まで」.
senses.connection: Noun + はもとより、noun + も／まで
examples: This festival draws not only locals but also many tourists from abroad.
For good health, sleep matters as well as diet, of course.

notes: The first item must be the obvious, more expected one, and the second the one that goes further. Reverse the order and the logic breaks: ✕「平日はもちろん、週末も混んでいる」→ ○「週末はもちろん、平日も混んでいる」.
The second clause needs 「も」, 「まで」, or 「さえ」 to match: ✕「味はもちろん、サービスがいい」→ ○「味はもちろん、サービスもいい」.
It follows a noun (or noun + particle). A verb must first be nominalized: ✕「話すはもちろん」→ ○「話すことはもちろん」.
The adverb 「もとより」 means “from the start” (「もとより承知の上だ」), and 「もちろん」 on its own means “of course” (「もちろんです」); neither is the “A goes without saying, and B too ...” pattern.
「はもとより」 is rather formal, used in speeches and notices; among friends it sounds stiff, so use 「はもちろん」 in daily life.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending a favorite place to a friend.
daily.example: That place has great ramen, of course, and the gyoza are good too.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: Introducing a talented friend to someone.
daily.example: She's a great singer, of course, and a great dancer too.

work.title: Presenting a product
work.description: Telling a client about a product's strengths.
work.example: This product is highly rated for its design, not to mention its performance.

work.title: Job requirements
work.description: Stating requirements in a job posting.
work.example: We welcome applicants who speak English as well as Japanese.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: At a year-end party, the company president thanks employees and their families.
work.example: We sincerely thank not only our employees but also all of your families.

etymology: 「もちろん」 is written 「勿論」, a word of Chinese origin meaning literally “no need to discuss”; combined with the topic particle 「は」 it says “this goes without saying” and then leads on to something further. 「もとより」 is written 「元より・固より」, made of 「もと（本・元）」 + 「より」, originally “from the beginning, originally”, extended from “that is how it was from the start” to “it goes without saying”.
formation: Built from the topic particle 「は」 + the adverb 「もちろん」 (勿論, literally “no need to discuss”) or 「もとより」 (元より, “it was so from the start”). 「は」 raises the first item A as the topic, and 「もちろん／もとより」 comments on it as “needless to say, naturally so”, i.e. “A needs no discussion (of course)”. The speaker first sets out A as an unquestionable example, then uses 「も」「まで」「さえ」 to bring in B, meaning “B is the same”, which gives the progressive structure “A goes without saying, and even B...” — the shared skeleton of all the senses here. Because A is labelled “obvious”, A must be the side that is easier to satisfy and B carries the new information. Adding 「のこと」 (「〜はもちろんのこと」) nominalizes the whole and sounds more formal; 「もとより」 is more refined than 「もちろん」, so it leans toward written style and speeches.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “not to mention ...”. 「〜は言うまでもなく」 is more written and more emphatic; 「〜はもちろん」 is more everyday.

similar.title: 〜は言うに及ばず
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but a more literary, stiff written expression, mostly seen in texts. In everyday conversation, use 「〜はもちろん」.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Both can mean “not only ... but also ...”. 「〜だけでなく」 simply widens the range, with no ranking between the items. 「〜はもちろん」 stresses that the first item is a given, and the second item is the real point.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Written-style “not only ... but also ...”; it only expresses an expanding range and, unlike 「はもとより」, does not stress that A is taken for granted.

similar.title: 〜はおろか
similar.explanation: Also “A goes without saying, even B ...”, but mostly used in negative or unfavorable contexts (「漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない」) with dissatisfaction or surprise; 「はもとより」 is mostly used in affirmative or neutral statements.

meaning: Sets something aside from the discussion for now. Like “leaving ... aside”, “apart from ...”, or “except for ...”.
connection: Noun + は別として／を別にして; question + かどうか(は)別として

senses.label: Leaving ... aside
senses.meaning: Ignores the first item for now and talks only about the second. Like “leaving ... aside” or “setting ... aside”. The first item is often minor or debatable.
senses.connection: Noun + は別として
examples: Price aside, the design is really good.
Joking aside, what are you actually going to do?

senses.label: Whether or not ...
senses.meaning: Follows a question to mean “whether or not ...”, treating it as not the issue. Like “regardless of whether ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + かどうかは別として／question word ... かは別として
examples: Whether or not I pass, I want to keep going until the end.
Regardless of who does it, the plan should move forward.

senses.label: Except for ...
senses.meaning: Excludes the first item as an exception. Like “except for ...”. You can also say 「〜を別にして」 or 「〜は別にして」.
senses.connection: Noun + は別として／を別にして
examples: Except for a few people, almost all employees agreed.
We're open every day except Sunday.

notes: With a question, use 「かどうか」 or a question word + 「か」: ✕「合格するは別として」→ ○「合格するかどうかは別として」 or 「誰が行くかは別として」.
When commenting on someone's proposal or work, saying 「デザインは別として…」 implies “that part isn't great”. To a client or superior this sounds rude. Phrase it positively instead: 「〜も素敵ですが、特に〜が…」.
Here 「別」 is read 「べつ」. The same kanji in 「別れる」 is read 「わかれる」 (to part, to say goodbye), so don't mix up the readings.

daily.title: Reviewing a movie
daily.description: Talking about a movie you just watched with a friend.
daily.example: Leaving the ending aside, the story was interesting.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend to enter a contest
daily.description: Telling a friend not to worry about the result.
daily.example: Whether you can win or not, why not give it a try?

work.title: Discussing a plan
work.description: In a meeting, setting the budget issue aside to discuss the content.
work.example: Budget issues aside, I think the plan itself is good.

work.title: HR explanation
work.description: Excluding special cases when explaining who is covered.
work.example: Except for managers, everyone is covered.

etymology: 「別」 means “separate” or “different”, and 「として」 means “as ...”. 「〜は別として」 means “treating ... as a separate matter”, so it sets something aside for now.

similar.title: 〜はともかく
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning: both mean “setting ... aside”. 「〜はともかく」 stresses more that the second part matters more than the first, and is common in speech. 「〜は別として」 focuses on “putting the first part aside as a separate matter”, and can also mark an exception, “except for ...”.

similar.title: 〜なら別だが
similar.explanation: Same origin (both use 「別」 for “a different story”). 「〜なら別だが」 is hypothetical: “if it's ..., that's a different story, but (generally) ...”. 「〜は別として」 has no hypothetical tone; it just puts the first part aside for now.

similar.title: 〜を除いて
similar.explanation: Close to the “except for ...” use. 「〜を除いて」 objectively excludes something and is written and formal. 「〜は別として」 not only excludes it but also implies an evaluation: “that part is a different story”.

formation: Made of the topic particle 「は」 + the noun 「別」 (separate, other) + 「として」 (“as ...”). 「Aは別として」 literally means “treating A as a separate matter”, that is, taking A out of the current discussion and setting it aside on its own. What is set aside can be a question you don't want to discuss now (“setting A aside”), something still uncertain (「〜かどうかは別として」 “whether or not ..., never mind for now”), or an exception that doesn't fit the overall picture (“except A”). Because A is only set aside, not denied, it often hints that A itself has problems or that the speaker has other views on it. 「として」 sounds fairly written; in speech it often becomes 「別にして」.

meaning: Shows that something is famous for a certain feature or thing. Like “famous for ...” or “known for ...”.
connection: Noun + で有名だ／で有名な + noun

senses.label: Famous for ...
senses.meaning: 「で」 marks the reason or feature something is famous for. Like “famous for ...” or “known for ...”. The subject is usually a place, person, or shop.
senses.connection: Noun + で有名だ／で有名です
examples: Kyoto is famous for its temples.
This town is famous for its hot springs.

senses.label: Noun famous for ...
senses.meaning: To modify a noun, use 「〜で有名な」: “a ... famous for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + で有名な + noun
examples: This is a restaurant famous for its ramen.
I went to a park famous for its cherry blossoms.

senses.label: Written: 〜で知られる
senses.meaning: 「〜で知られる」 and 「〜で知られている」 are more written versions with the same meaning. They are common in the news and in descriptions.
senses.connection: Noun + で知られる／で知られている
examples: This region is known as a rice-growing area, and also for its sake brewing.

notes: For a role or status, use 「として」, not 「で」: ✕「彼は歌手で有名だ」→ ○「彼は歌手として有名だ」. What comes before 「で」 is the reason or feature that made someone famous (「歌で有名」).
「有名」 is a na-adjective, so it modifies nouns as 「有名な」: ✕「有名の店」→ ○「有名な店」, 「ラーメンで有名な店」.
Using it for a person's negative trait (「彼はケチで有名だ」) is a public negative judgment. Saying it in front of the person, or in front of their company or hometown, is very rude.
「で」 can also mark a place: 「地元で有名な店」 means “a shop famous in the local area”, not “famous because of the local area”. Judge from the noun before it.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Talking with a friend about where to travel.
daily.example: Hokkaido is famous for seafood, so I'd like to go.

daily.title: Introducing your hometown
daily.description: Telling a friend from abroad about your hometown.
daily.example: My hometown is famous for apples.

daily.title: Watching a travel show
daily.description: A TV program introducing a sightseeing spot.
daily.example: This village is known for its beautiful rice terraces.

work.title: Hosting a client
work.description: Taking a client to a famous local restaurant.
work.example: This restaurant is famous for its tempura.

work.title: Writing a company profile
work.description: Introducing a partner company in materials.
work.example: The company is known for its high level of technical expertise.

etymology: 「有名」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “having a name (reputation)”. The particle 「で」 marks a cause or means, so 「〜で有名」 means “famous by way of ...”.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: 「〜として有名」 is often compared with 「〜で有名」. 「として」 shows a role or standpoint (“famous as ...”): 「作家として有名」. 「で」 shows the reason or feature for fame: 「小説で有名」.

similar.title: 〜て・〜で (cause)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「で」 in 「〜で有名」 is the 「で」 of cause (「病気で休む」). 「〜で有名」 is the fixed combination it forms with 「有名」.

formation: Made of the case particle 「で」 (cause, means) + the na-adjective 「有名」 (a Sino-Japanese word: having a name, renowned). 「Aで有名」 means “famous by virtue of A”: A is the reason or feature that made the subject famous, and the subject (a place, person, shop) is what is famous. Since 「有名」 is a na-adjective, the sentence ends in 「有名だ／です」, and it modifies nouns as 「〜で有名な + noun」. Replace 「有名だ」 with the passive 「知られている」 (to be known by people) and you get the more written 「〜で知られている」, with exactly the same structure.

meaning: Adds another situation of the same kind on top of the first. Like “not only ... but also ...” or “on top of ...”.
connection: Verb, i-adjective plain form／na-adjective + な・である／noun + の・である + 上に

senses.label: Not only ... but also (good + good)
senses.meaning: Adds a second point of the same kind to the first. Like “not only ... but also ...”. Both are positive, often with 「も」 in the second half.
senses.connection: Plain form + 上に、〜も
examples: This restaurant is not only cheap, but also tasty.
She's not only smart, but also kind.
This room is not only quiet, but also gets lots of sunlight.

senses.label: On top of that (bad + bad)
senses.meaning: Both sides are negative: one bad thing after another. Like “not only ..., but on top of that ...”. Often with 「まで」 or 「も」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form／plain form + 上に、〜まで
examples: Not only did I get lost, but it started raining too.
Yesterday I overslept, and on top of that I forgot my wallet.

notes: Both parts must point the same way (good + good, or bad + bad): ✕「この店は安い上に、まずい」→ ○「この店は安いけれど、まずい」.
The second clause cannot be a command, request, invitation, or intention: ✕「疲れている上に、早く寝なさい」→ ○「疲れているんだから、早く寝なさい」.
「〜上で」 differs by just one particle, but the meaning is completely different: 「よく考えた上で決める」 = decide after thinking it over carefully; ✕「よく考えた上に決める」.
After a noun, use 「である」 (or 「の」): ○「新人である上に」. Written as 「新人の上に」, it can easily be read as a location, “on top of the newcomer”.

daily.title: Recommending an apartment
daily.description: Recommending a place you viewed to a friend.
daily.example: That room is spacious, and the rent is cheap too.

daily.title: Complaining about a bad day
daily.description: Telling your family what happened today.
daily.example: The train was late, and on top of that I forgot my umbrella and got soaked.

daily.title: Praising a new classmate
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about a transfer student.
daily.example: That kid is not only good at sports, but good at studying too.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: HR reporting on a new employee to a manager.
work.example: He not only works fast, but also makes few mistakes.

work.title: Explaining project difficulties
work.description: Reporting the problems a project faces to your boss.
work.example: We're short-staffed, and on top of that our budget was cut.

etymology: 「上」 originally means “above”, and extends to “adding on top of ...”. 「〜上に」 stacks one more layer on top of an existing situation, so it shows addition.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Both mean “not only ... but also ...”. 「〜だけでなく」 simply widens the range, and the second clause can be a request or invitation (「見るだけでなく、触ってみてください」). 「〜上に」 stresses piling up things that point the same way, and the second clause can only state facts.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: Both can add up circumstances. 「〜し」 is common in speech, can list several items in a row, and often implies a reason. 「〜上に」 usually links just two items, is a bit more written, and stresses “on top of that”.

similar.title: 〜上(に)
similar.explanation: The same expression as this one (reviewed at N2 with a focus on written use): 「に」 can be dropped, giving 「〜上、」, which is common in texts.

similar.title: 〜上で
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built on 「上」), but different meaning: 「〜た上で」 means “after ... (then ...)”, and 「〜上で」 means “in terms of ...”. Neither expresses addition.

formation: Made of the formal noun 「上（うえ）」 + the case particle 「に」. 「上」 basically means “top, above”, and 「Aの上に」 originally means “(put something) on top of A”. Applied from space to situations, it becomes “stack B on top of situation A”, i.e. adding a similar situation to an existing one. Because it is “stacking on top”, what you add should point the same way as what was there, so it can only be “good on top of good” or “bad on top of bad”. And because it is an objective adding-up of facts, the second clause is usually not a command, request, or other expression of the speaker's will.

meaning: Shows that something is not limited to the first item but extends to the second. Like “not only ... but also ...”.
connection: Noun／verb, adjective plain form (na-adjective + な) + だけでなく

senses.label: Not only A, but also B
senses.meaning: The scope isn't limited to the first item; it extends to the second. Like “not only ..., but also ...”. The second half often has 「も」 or 「まで」.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + だけでなく、〜も
examples: He can speak not only English, but also French.
This book is popular not only with children, but also with adults.
It's important not just to watch, but to actually try it.

senses.label: Casual forms
senses.meaning: In speech, people often say 「〜だけじゃなくて」 or 「〜だけじゃなく」. In writing, 「〜だけではなく」 is also used. The meaning is the same.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + だけじゃなくて／だけではなく
examples: It's not just the taste. It looks beautiful too.
I'm working hard not only at my studies, but also in my club.

senses.label: It's not just ...
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, 「〜だけではない」 means “it's not just ... (there's more)”.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + だけではない／だけじゃない
examples: Money isn't the only problem.
His charm isn't just his looks.

notes: The second clause needs 「も」, 「まで」, etc. to match: ✕「英語だけでなく、フランス語が話せる」→ ○「英語だけでなく、フランス語も話せる」.
Drop 「なく」 and the meaning changes completely: 「見るだけでなく」 = not only looking; 「見るだけで楽しい」 = just looking is fun.
A na-adjective needs 「な」, and a noun attaches directly: ✕「便利だけでなく」→ ○「便利なだけでなく」; ✕「学生のだけでなく」→ ○「学生だけでなく」.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a talented friend to someone.
daily.example: She's not only a good singer, but good at piano too.

daily.title: Recommending a spot
daily.description: Recommending a local spot to tourists.
daily.example: It's not just the scenery here. The food is delicious too.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Discussing the benefits of exercise with family.
daily.example: Exercise is good not only for your body, but also for your mind.

work.title: Product presentation
work.description: Explaining a product's strengths to clients.
work.example: We are confident not only in the price of this product, but also in its quality.

work.title: In-house training
work.description: A trainer explaining job expectations to new employees.
work.example: Not only knowledge, but also the ability to put it into practice is required.

etymology: It combines 「だけ」 (limit), 「で」, and 「なく」, the linking form of the negative 「ない」. Literally “not just ...”, it came to mean “not only ... (but also ...)”.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning. 「〜ばかりでなく」 is slightly more written; 「〜だけでなく」 works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but written language, mostly seen in texts and speeches. In everyday conversation, use 「〜だけでなく」.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: Also means “not limited to ...”, but focuses on “others of the same kind are the same”: 「日本に限らず、多くの国で」. 「〜だけでなく」 just adds B on top of A.

similar.title: 〜上に
similar.explanation: 「〜上に」 stresses piling up things that point the same way (good on top of good, or one bad thing after another), and the second clause only states facts. 「〜だけでなく」 just widens the range, and the second clause can also be a request or invitation.

formation: Made of the limiting adverbial particle 「だけ」 (only, just) + 「で」 (the continuative form of the copula 「だ」) + 「なく」 (the continuative form of the negative 「ない」). 「Aだけだ」 is “only A”, and negating it as 「Aだけではない」 gives “not only A”. The suspended form 「なく」 links to the next clause and brings in B, which lies outside that range, giving “not only A, B too ...”. It just breaks the limitation and widens the range, with no “of course” or “piling up in the same direction” nuance of its own, so it is wider in use and more neutral than 「〜上に」 or 「〜はもちろん」.

meaning: Emphasizes the word before it: “this is exactly ...” or “this, and nothing else”.
connection: Noun + こそ; 〜から／〜て + こそ

senses.label: Exactly / precisely
senses.meaning: Emphasizes one thing: “not anything else, but exactly this”. Like “this is the very ...” or “... is what really matters”. Stronger than 「は」 or 「が」.
senses.connection: Noun + こそ
examples: This is exactly the book I was looking for.
Health is the most valuable asset of all.

senses.label: This time for sure
senses.meaning: With time words like 「今度」, 「今年」, or 「次」, it shows strong determination. Like “this time for sure”.
senses.connection: 今度／今年／明日 + こそ + expression of will
examples: This year I really want to pass the JLPT.
This time I won't lose!

senses.label: I'm the one who ... (greeting)
senses.meaning: 「こちらこそ」 answers someone's thanks or apology: “No, I should be the one thanking/apologizing”. Like “likewise” or “the pleasure is mine”.
senses.connection: こちらこそ + よろしくお願いします／ありがとうございます, etc.
examples: “Nice to meet you.” “Nice to meet you too.”

senses.label: Precisely because ...
senses.meaning: 「〜からこそ」 stresses the reason: “precisely because ...”. 「〜てこそ」 means “only by doing ... can you ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + からこそ／verb te-form + こそ
examples: It's precisely because I like you that I'm being strict with you.
Only by trying it yourself do you understand how hard it really is.

notes: 「あなたこそ」 and 「お前こそ」 fire back at the other person, “No, YOU are ...!”. The tone is aggressive, so never use them with a superior or client. The only polite use is the set phrase 「こちらこそ（よろしくお願いします／すみません）」.
「こちらこそ」 is only a response to the other person's thanks, apology, or greeting; you can't use it if they haven't said anything first: they say 「ありがとう」 → ○「こちらこそ」.
「こそ」 does not stack with 「は」, 「が」, or 「を」: ✕「これがこそ」→ ○「これこそ」. But it can follow 「で」, 「に」, 「から」, etc. (「ここでこそ」, 「だからこそ」).
「〜からこそ」 cannot be replaced with 「ので」: ✕「好きなのでこそ」→ ○「好きだからこそ」.

daily.title: Meeting someone for the first time
daily.description: Replying when the other person says 「よろしく」.
daily.example: Likewise, nice to meet you.

daily.title: New Year's resolutions
daily.description: Telling a friend your goal for the year.
daily.example: This year I'm quitting smoking for sure!

daily.title: When a friend apologizes
daily.description: A friend apologizes for being late, but you were also at fault.
daily.example: No, I'm the one who should apologize.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Encouraging the team in a meeting after a failure.
work.example: Let's make sure it succeeds this time.

work.title: Thanking a client
work.description: Replying formally after a client thanks you.
work.example: Not at all, we're the ones who are always grateful for your support.

etymology: 「こそ」 is an emphasis particle that goes back to Classical Japanese. In old texts, it paired with a special verb ending at the end of the sentence (the 「こそ〜已然形」 pattern). Modern Japanese keeps its emphatic function.

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「から」 + 「こそ」, used specifically to stress a reason (“precisely because ...”). 「こそ」 on its own can stress any noun.

similar.title: 〜てこそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「て」 + 「こそ」, stresses a condition, meaning “only by ... can ...”: 「やってみてこそ分かる」.

similar.title: 〜ばこそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ば」 + 「こそ」. Close in meaning to 「からこそ」 (“precisely because ...”), but more literary and written, and usually gives a well-meant reason.

similar.title: 〜こそ〜が (concession)
similar.explanation: Same origin but a different use: 「こそ」 pairs with 「が」 to make a concession, “... is true, but ...” (「値段こそ高いが、品質はいい」). It is not simple emphasis.

formation: 「こそ」 is a binding particle (kakarijoshi) that already existed in classical Japanese, used specifically to “single out” one item and emphasize it. After a noun, it picks that item out from all the possibilities, implying “not anything else, exactly this”, so 「これこそ」 = “this, exactly”. Combined with 「今度」 or 「今年」, it singles out “this time” from all past failures, giving the resolve “this time for sure”. 「こちらこそ」 singles out “my side”, meaning “I'm the one who should be saying that”. After 「から」, 「て」, or 「ば」, what it singles out is a reason or condition, giving 「からこそ」, 「てこそ」, and 「ばこそ」. In classical Japanese, 「こそ」 required the sentence to end in the realis form (kakari-musubi); modern Japanese keeps only its emphasizing function.
